items.title: Seven of our 32 called, all Democrats, four of them flips
items.body:
Called so far: FL-14, FL-22, FL-25 (holds) and VA-2 Luria, KY-6 Dembo, NC-11 Ager, PA-8 Cognetti (flips from Republican). Of the 19 board races with votes and no call, Democrats lead 12; eleven of those leads would be flips if they hold (VA-1, NY-17, CO-5, OH-7, WI-3, PA-10, MO-2, PA-1, IA-2, plus Republicans leading in OH-9 Kaptur and AL-2 Figures, the two Democratic-held seats at risk). Board CAPE score: Democrats running +4.5 points ahead of DDHQ's forecasts on average across 26 races.
Caveat to say out loud: the early-counted ballots (mail, early in-person) lean Democratic in most of these states; expect Republican-leaning Election Day batches to narrow margins over the next hour. OH-9 and AL-2 are at 44% counted.

items.title: The tide: Democrats +7.5 points vs. 2024 in 395 counties
items.body: Across the 395 counties on the caucus lists that are at least half counted, the two-party vote is running 7.5 points more Democratic than the 2024 presidential vote in the same counties. For scale: 2018's national House swing against the president's party was about 10 points off the 2016 presidential margin. Turnout is coming in about as expected on both sides (live expected vote vs. pre-election: Harris counties −0.2%, Trump counties +1%), so this is a persuasion-and-midterm-dropoff swing, not a differential-turnout story.

items.title: Senate: 17 called; Democrats leading in every Toss Up with votes
items.body:
Called: South Carolina Andrews (D, flip) and North Carolina Cooper (D, flip) among 12 Democratic calls; Republicans hold FL (Moody), KY (Barr), OK, WV, WY. Not called, Democrat ahead: Ohio Brown 48.3–47.0 (66% in), Texas Talarico 56–42 (66%), Kansas Hamilton 58–40 (63%), Iowa Turek 59–39 (24%), Michigan El-Sayed 54–44 (20%), Louisiana Davis (5%, ignore). Nebraska: independent Osborn 54–41.5 over Ricketts at 42%. Republicans ahead: Maine Collins 51.5–47.7 at 21%, Mississippi Hyde-Smith 50.1–47.9 at 49%, Tennessee Hagerty 51.5–47.7 at 50%, Arkansas Cotton only 49.2–47.9 at 36%.
If every current leader held, Democrats plus Osborn would have the majority. Say it as 'if every leader held' — Ohio, Texas, Kansas and Iowa are early-vote-heavy counts.

items.title: Caucus scoreboards: every Democratic list is beating its forecasts; Blue Dogs +10 in competitive seats
items.body: Blue Dogs: 6 won, 2 lost, 10 leading, 3 trailing; CAPE score +9.8 across 21 races with votes. In competitive seats (forecast within 10 points) at least half counted, Blue Dog candidates are beating their forecasts by 10.2 points vs. +7.9 for other Democrats in the same kind of seat (11 vs. 60 races) — the defensible 'Blue Dog premium' is about 2 points, not the raw 10. DCCC Red to Blue: 8 won, 1 lost, 14 leading. Progressive Caucus slate: 1 won, 3 leading, 3 trailing, +4.8. Republican lists: NRCC MAGA Majority 0 won, 9 lost, 3 leading, 8 trailing, −7.7 vs. forecast; Main Street Republicans 0–4, −4.9. Texas governor: Hinojosa (D) 55–45 over Abbott at 63% counted, rated Lean R; Georgia governor called for the Democrat, a flip.

items.title: No rain tax tonight: the CAPE Rain Tax is about zero
items.body: H1 across 1,369 counties at least half counted: each inch of rain goes with +0.5% votes vs. expectation (p = 0.33; 95% CI −0.5 to +1.5). The literature's roughly −2% per inch (Gomez, Hansford & Krause) is outside that interval, so tonight's data don't show the classic rain penalty. H2 (the rules line): rain is going with 3.6% LESS shortfall on the restrictive-voting side than the convenience-voting side — opposite the hypothesis; small sample (297 counties, 14 state pairs). H4 (ballot type within county) and H5 (county size): no signal. Say it as: 336 wet counties, mostly in the central U.S. system over KS–MO–IA–WI and south Texas, and people voted anyway — or they'd already voted by mail.

items.title: 7:15 · The tide: 123 of 126 districts have moved toward Democrats since 2024, median +17 points
items.body:
On unchanged lines, at least half counted: 126 districts compare with their 2024 House result. 123 moved toward Democrats, 3 toward Republicans; the median shift is +17.4 points in Democratic margin (safe-R seats +18.5, lean-R +19.3, lean-D +19.4, safe-D +13.7). The 25 districts at 90%+ counted show the same +17.2, so it isn't only an early-vote mirage. By county, the caucus-list counties at least half counted are +7.5 vs. the 2024 presidential; every county in the feed, +15 (Harris counties +17, Trump counties +14; Democrats are taking 43% of the vote in Trump counties tonight vs. 36% in 2024).
Caveat: a House margin vs. a presidential margin exaggerates swings in safe seats where the out-party ran weak in 2024. The district-vs-district number is the one to quote.

items.title: 7:30 · Turnout: fully counted counties are at 110% of 2022 and 78% of 2024, red and blue alike
items.body:
In the 55 tracked counties that report all votes counted (Virginia, Kentucky, Florida, Ohio, Georgia), votes cast are 110% of 2022's total and 78% of 2024's. Harris counties: 108% of 2022; Trump counties: 112% of 2022 — the Trump counties are turning out slightly MORE relative to 2022, which is why the blue tide is a persuasion story, not a turnout story. Against DDHQ's pre-election expectation, counties at least half counted are running +0.4% (Harris) and +1.5% (Trump). Highest vs. 2022: Paulding OH 135%, Williamsburg VA 134%, Goochland VA 127%; lowest: Fayette KY 95%, Fleming KY 92%. Caveat: 'fully counted' is DDHQ's flag and late mail can still add a few percent; Virginia's small counties dominate this sample.
Traffic: 686 views and 262 visitors on the lab pages as of 7:01pm; a quarter arrived from Instagram.
items.show: Turnout tab (fully counted only, vs 2022); then Weather & turnout ↗ for the expectation comparison

items.title: 7:45 · Rain tax update: −0.01% per inch across 1,832 counties — nothing
items.body: The CAPE Rain Tax is now measured on 1,832 counties at least half counted, 569 of them with at least a millimeter of rain today: each inch of rain goes with −0.01% of expected vote (p = 0.98; 95% CI −1.1 to +1.0). The classic Gomez–Hansford–Krause estimate (about −2% per inch, in presidential years) sits outside that interval. The one test with a signal is H2, and it points the wrong way: within 100 km of a rules line, rain goes with 3% LESS shortfall on the side that requires an excuse to vote by mail (p < 0.05, 370 counties, 14 state pairs) — the simplest reading is that heavy-rain counties tonight happen to be high-turnout counties, not that rules matter in reverse. H3 (does rain shift the partisan split?): +0.04 points per cm, nothing. H4 (Election Day ballots vs. the county's early ballots): +0.2%, nothing; placebo also nothing. H5 (county size): no interaction (p = 0.11). Caveat: 'expected vote' is DDHQ's live estimate, which moves with the count; the final read comes when counts close.
items.show: Weather & turnout ↗ → Jump to the hypothesis tests; H1 figure, then H2

items.title: 8:10 · California's first batch: Becerra 55–45, Prop 39 (voter ID) failing 49.6–50.4, Prop 44 crushed
items.body: The 8:03pm batch (pre-election mail, 6% of precincts, about 610,000 governor votes): Becerra 55.1%, Hilton 44.9% — short of the PPIC 61–37 and Emerson 60–33 polls, but the first batch is the oldest electorate California counts; later mail skews younger. Propositions, same batch: Prop 3 (extend the high-income tax for schools and health care) yes 52.8%; Prop 1 (housing bonds) yes 53.3%; Prop 39 (government-issued ID to vote) NO 50.4–49.6, the one to watch; Prop 40 (one-time wealth tax) no 63.5%; Prop 44 (clinics' 90% rule) no 81.5%; Prop 42 (no new personal-property taxes) yes 63.0%; Prop 2 (rainy-day fund) dead even, 50.4 yes. BOE District 1: Esparza 53.7%, Grove 46.3% at 16% (open seat). Caveat: California's first drop is pre-election mail only; in 2022 and 2024 the Election Day batches moved Valley races several points toward Republicans before late mail moved them back.

items.title: 8:12 · CA-13 first batch: Gray 58.8–41.2 on 39,000 votes
items.body: Secretary of State, 8:05pm: Gray 23,072 (58.8%), Lincoln 16,134 (41.2%) — 39,206 votes, roughly a fifth of the ~200,000 expected. The SoS's '83% of precincts reporting' means mail has been counted from most precincts, not that 83% of the vote is in. Same-count check against his past races (the tracker on /ca13): at this stage in 2024 Gray led by about 1.3 points and finished +0.1; in 2022 the morning-after count matched the final within 0.1. Tonight's first batch is about 17 points better than 2024's first batch. Lincoln would need roughly 55% of the remaining vote to catch up; in 2024 Duarte's best batch, the Election Day in-person count, ran about 56% for him. The lab's pre-8pm projection from the national tide was Gray 54–56%; this batch is above it. Caveat: one batch, oldest voters; Merced's Election Day count lands around 11:30.

items.title: 8:30 · CAPE alumni: Brandon trails 46.6–53.4 in SD-4 at 47%; Rascón's SD-26 hasn't reported
items.body: SD-4 (open seat, Alvarado-Gil out): Jaron Brandon (D) 46,364 to Alexandra Duarte (R) 53,083 — 46.6% to 53.4% with 47% of precincts reporting, per the Secretary of State's 8:19pm batch. The district runs from the foothills through Stanislaus's east side; the mail-first batches here lean older and more Republican than the Election Day in-person vote did in 2024, so the gap can narrow, but seven points is a lot to make up with half the precincts in. SD-26 (open, Los Angeles): Sarah Rascón vs. Sara Hernandez, both Democrats, 0 of 155 precincts — LA County posts its first batch later than the Valley counties. Caveat: the SoS percent is precincts partially reporting, not share of the vote.

items.title: 9:10 · Merced County: Esparza 57.8% in BOE-1 here, Gray 57.7%, Pacheco 61% in AD-27 — and the county's own site still hasn't posted
items.body: Merced County's first mail batch (all 770 precincts touched, per the Secretary of State): Board of Equalization District 1, Esparza 19,271 (57.8%) to Grove 14,065 in Merced; districtwide Esparza 55.0% at 46% of precincts, with Madera (Grove 52.2%), Mariposa and Tuolumne leaning Grove and Stanislaus 53.0% Esparza. CA-13 in Merced: Gray 19,368 (57.7%) to Lincoln 14,224, six points better than his 51.4% Merced finish in 2024. AD-27's Merced piece: Pacheco 18,864 (61.0%) to Murphy 12,047. SD-4's small Merced piece: Duarte 1,683 to Brandon 1,337. County contests and the eight local measures: Merced's own results site (Clarity) still lists no election as of 9:05, so the Merced County tab shows the ballot list without numbers; early in-person was due at 9:30 and Election Day in-person at 11:30 on the county's schedule. The lab checks it every cycle.

items.title: 9:15 · Decision Desk HQ has called CA-13 for Adam Gray
items.body: DDHQ called it at 9:12pm: Gray 42,049 (60.7%), Lincoln 27,190 (39.3%) with about 45% of the expected vote in. Two years ago this seat was decided by 187 votes; tonight's first batches are running about 17 points better for Gray than 2024's first batches, and Merced's Election Day count (around 11:30) would have to swing more than 20 points the other way to matter. Same-count check: at this stage in 2024 Gray led by 1.3. On the lab: the race card flipped to Winner; the CA-13 page has county rows.

items.title: 9:15 · Blue Dogs: running about 2 points ahead of the rest of the Democratic ticket, 5 pickups already
items.body: Blue Dog candidates with at least half the vote counted are beating Decision Desk HQ's pre-election forecast by 8.6 points on average (23 of 25 ahead of forecast); the average Democrat in the same kind of race is beating it by 6.7. In competitive seats only (forecast within 10), 7.6 vs 5.7. Pickups called so far: AZ-6 Mendoza, KY-6 Dembo, NC-11 Ager, PA-7 Brooks, TX-15 Pulido. Also won: Cuellar, Gonzalez, Gottheimer, Costa, Correa, Gray, Bishop. Leading in uncalled Republican seats: CO-3, CO-4, NJ-2, NC-13, SC-1, WI-1, WI-3. Lost: FL-2, FL-13, KS-2. Trailing narrowly: FL-7, MN-1, NY-21, TN-5. Say it carefully: a 2-point premium on top of a 7-point wave, in the seats Republicans needed.

items.title: 9:30 · Where the night stands: Democrats 2 seats from the House, 52 called in the Senate
items.body: Decision Desk HQ as of 9:25pm. House: 216 D, 125 R called; 24 Democratic pickups, zero Republican pickups; 90 races uncalled, Democrats leading 46 of them. Senate: 18 D, 9 R called; six Democratic pickups (Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Texas), none the other way. With 34 Democratic seats not on the ballot that is 52 called for a Democratic Senate, with Maine (Jackson 53%) and Mississippi (Colom 49.6% at 92%) still open. California governor: Becerra 64%, 44% of precincts. Props: voter ID (39) failing 41–59; the one-time wealth tax (40) failing; rainy-day fund, housing bonds and the high-income tax extension passing around 58–59%. The lab's tide measure across 640 counties: D+6.8. The honest caveat: the House majority is not called yet, and California, Arizona and Washington mail will decide the final margin over the next week.
